# Get started on the Nucleo-F767ZI

<!-- type: how-to · level: 1 -->

**Needs first:** [Install](../start/install.md)

This starter puts a C talker on an ST Nucleo-F767ZI (STM32F767ZI, Cortex-M7)
running Zephyr 3.7, talking to ROS 2 over the board's USB serial port. You do
not need the board to start: [Renode](https://renode.io) emulates it on your
machine, and wires USART3, the UART the Nucleo's ST-LINK carries to your USB
port, to your host the way the cable would. The image you run in Renode is
the image you later flash to the board.

## What you need

- A Linux x86_64 host with the [install](../start/install.md) done, so `nros`
  is on your `PATH`, and ROS 2 Humble with `ros-humble-rmw-zenoh-cpp`.
- For the last step only: a Nucleo-F767ZI and a USB cable for its ST-LINK
  port. Everything before it runs in the twin.
- Zephyr's host tools: `west` and the build tools
  [Zephyr's Getting Started](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/3.7.0/develop/getting_started/index.html)
  lists. `nros setup` installs no system packages, so install them yourself.
  On Debian or Ubuntu:

```bash probe=30 track=installed
sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends git cmake ninja-build gperf \
    device-tree-compiler python3-pip python3-venv xz-utils file wget
pip3 install --user west
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
```

The serial link comes first and is the only link this starter opens.
Ethernet is covered under [Next](#next). WiFi is deferred to the Zephyr 4.4
line, so no starter opens over WiFi yet.

## Provision

Provision the board:

```bash probe=32 track=installed
nros setup nucleo-f767zi-zephyr --rmw zenoh
export ZEPHYR_SDK_INSTALL_DIR="$(nros locate tool zephyr-sdk)"
```

That fetches what the board needs into a shared store under `~/.nros`: the
Zephyr SDK, the zenoh-pico sources, the Rust target, and Renode. It installs
no router: the router is ROS's `rmw_zenohd`, from your ROS 2 install.

Zephyr's sources live in a west workspace of your own. This one pins Zephyr
3.7 and fetches only the modules the board builds with, `hal_stm32` among them
(`import: true` would fetch every vendor's HAL):

```bash probe=34 track=installed
mkdir -p nucleo_ws/manifest && cd nucleo_ws
cat > manifest/west.yml <<'WEST_YML'
manifest:
  remotes:
    - name: zephyrproject-rtos
      url-base: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos
  projects:
    - name: zephyr
      remote: zephyrproject-rtos
      revision: v3.7.0
      import:
        name-allowlist: [cmsis, picolibc, mbedtls, tinycrypt, mcuboot, net-tools, hal_stm32]
    # Zephyr's Rust support. The board's setup patches it, so the workspace
    # needs it even for a C talker. Pinned to the revision nano-ros builds
    # with on the 3.7 line (it has no release tags).
    - name: zephyr-lang-rust
      remote: zephyrproject-rtos
      revision: 404fcefdbab0f2711cd342a1fab9d2eda52a1ba9
      path: modules/lang/rust
  self:
    path: manifest
WEST_YML
west init -l manifest
west update --narrow -o=--depth=1
pip3 install --user -r zephyr/scripts/requirements-base.txt
export ZEPHYR_BASE="$PWD/zephyr"
```

Last, give the west workspace the patches nano-ros carries for Zephyr 3.7:

```bash probe=36 track=installed
nros setup board nucleo-f767zi-zephyr --zephyr-workspace "$PWD"
```

## Scaffold the project

```bash probe=40 track=installed
nros new nucleo_ws --board nucleo-f767zi-zephyr --template talker --lang c
cd nucleo_ws
```

That wrote a workspace with two packages: `src/nucleo_node/`, the C talker,
and `src/nucleo_node_bringup/`, which says what the talker runs on. The board
reaches the router on your host through USART3, which Zephyr calls
`serial@40004800`, at 115200 baud. Say so with one line at the end of the
bringup's `system.toml`:

```bash probe=45 track=installed
echo 'locator = "serial/serial@40004800#baudrate=115200"' >> src/nucleo_node_bringup/system.toml
```

The line lands in the `[image.zephyr]` block, under the
`board = "nucleo-f767zi-zephyr"` line the scaffold wrote. The board's own
configuration already turns Zephyr's IP stack off and gives USART3 to zenoh.
Its console is USART6.

## Run it in the Renode twin

Source ROS 2, then build and run. ROS 2 provides the router, and its message
definitions are what the build generates the talker's `std_msgs` code from.
This first run records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace, so later runs of it
need no sourced shell:

```bash probe=50 probe-run=1500 track=installed
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run nucleo_node --expect 'Publishing:'
```

```text probe-expect=50
Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
nros run: matched after
```

`nros run` builds the firmware through west (the first build takes a few
minutes; later ones take seconds), boots it in Renode's `nucleo_f767zi`
machine with USART3 on a terminal device of your host, starts `rmw_zenohd` on
that device, and prints the board's console, USART6. With `--expect` it stops
everything and exits 0 at the first console line containing that text, and
exits 1 if the board stops first.

Without `--expect` it keeps running until you press Ctrl-C. Start it that way
in one terminal:

```bash probe=60 probe-run=300 probe-keep track=installed
nros run nucleo_node
```

```text probe-expect=60
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'
```

## Flash the board

On the bench, plug the Nucleo's ST-LINK port into your host and flash the
same image:

```bash
nros flash --monitor
```

> **Not replayed.** No probe runs this flash line (a CI runner has no board), so it is written from the board's runner, not measured ([tracking issue](https://github.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/blob/main/docs/issues/archived/2176-unprobed-fvp-sitl-flash-lines.md)).

`nros flash` builds the image if it is stale and programs it through
Zephyr's own runner for the board, OpenOCD over the ST-LINK. With
`--monitor` it then serves the board's link on your host: on the real board
USART3 is the ST-LINK's virtual COM port, so the zenoh link arrives as a USB
serial device (`/dev/ttyACM0`, say), and the router listens there instead of
on Renode's terminal device. Name the device with `--port` when more than one
is attached. The console, USART6, is on the board's pins, not on the USB
cable.

## See it in ROS 2

With the talker running, in the twin or on the board, ask ROS 2 for the topic
from a second terminal. The router `nros run` started
also listens where a ROS 2 node on this machine looks for one, so nothing
needs to be configured:

```bash probe=70 probe-run=120 track=installed
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort
```

```text probe-expect=70
data: 'Hello World:
```

The talker publishes best-effort, so the echo asks for best-effort too.
Ctrl-C in the first terminal stops Renode and the router together.

## If it doesn't work

- **`nros run` names `no runner package drives` or `the plan's tools name no
  renode`:** run the `nros setup nucleo-f767zi-zephyr` step again, which
  installs Renode.
- **A router that does not start:** `rmw_zenohd` was not found (source ROS 2
  in that terminal), or another router already holds port 7447 on this
  machine.
- **A build that cannot find `hal_stm32`:** the west workspace predates the
  `hal_stm32` line in its allowlist. Add it and run `west update` again.
- **Everything else:** [Troubleshooting - First 10 Minutes](../reference/troubleshooting-index.md).

## Next

- **Ethernet.** The Nucleo's on-chip ethernet MAC works in Renode: the talker
  reached a router over `tcp/` with Zephyr's `eth_stm32_hal` driver in an
  early spike. That run needed a host tap device bridged to Renode's virtual
  switch, which takes `CAP_NET_ADMIN`, and `nros run` does not set one up
  yet, so this starter stops at serial.
